verdict.reason: Both debates converge on the same sound plan (pause, settle, reintroduce singly, with a medical exit ramp), but A's objections do more work: the combination problem, the weakness of forearm patch tests for facial skin, and the need to define in advance what counts as a reaction each change the method rather than restate it. B's distinctive move is a motive-reading of the user that it then contests and turns into a useful branch, but it leaves the patch test and the stacked-actives possibility unexamined.

comparisons.a_observation: The Subtractor raises that products may be fine singly and harsh together, so single reintroduction could acquit every product; later it attacks the Experimenter's forearm patch test (facial skin reacts differently) and the risk of restarting the clock, and the Experimenter explicitly concedes the slower trial while holding the line on reintroduction.
comparisons.b_observation: The retest-too-soon objection narrows the Experimenter's claim to a clean baseline, and the Skeptic adds a replication point, but the Experimenter's own patch-test proposal goes unchallenged and no one considers interaction between products.
comparisons.why_it_matters: Three products started at once is exactly the case where a stacked combination can be the cause and where a weak patch test can mislead, so A's objections change what the user would actually do (test pairs if singles are clean; do not trust the forearm alone).

comparisons.a_observation: Turns the vague word 'sting' into a measurement problem: decide beforehand what counts (lasting redness, burning after rinsing, flaking) and log at ten minutes and an hour; dependsOn offers dropping a non-essential product as a legitimate cheaper path.
comparisons.b_observation: Offers a speculative reading of the user's motives, which the Subtractor contests from the user's actual wording, and the Experimenter converts the two readings into different advice (rescue products vs. just get comfortable).
comparisons.why_it_matters: A sharpens the user's 'figure out what's causing it' into observable criteria; B ties the depth of investigation to what the user wants, which is also decision-relevant. Each helps on a different axis.

comparisons.a_observation: Branches on fading vs. not fading, other changes that week, red-flag symptoms, and whether a product is essential; reintroduce one every one to two weeks.
comparisons.b_observation: Branches on severity (including trouble breathing), mild and fading, comfort-only goals, and adds that a sting not easing after a week or two of a minimal routine warrants a dermatologist.
comparisons.why_it_matters: Both give the user observable conditions; B's persistent-sting-to-dermatologist branch and A's combination-testing branch are each a real addition the other lacks.

verdict.best_of_a: A.debate[4].text: The point that single-product retesting can acquit every product while the combination (e.g. two layered exfoliating acids) is the cause, with the concrete fix of testing pairs if singles come back clean.
verdict.best_of_b: B.debate[7].text: The Experimenter turns the contested reading of the user's motives into a branch: a slow test is worth it if the user wants to rescue products, poor value if they only want comfort, with the clinician exit applying to both.

concerns.description: Speculates about the user's hopes and fears about the products without basis in the input; it is labelled as rejectable and contested in the next turn, so the effect is limited.
Recommends a forearm or behind-the-ear patch test as the first step without noting that facial skin may react differently, which could give false reassurance.
Red-flag list omits breathing difficulty as an urgent-care trigger and draws no urgency distinction between seeing a doctor or pharmacist and emergency care.

verdict.reason: Both debates converge on calm-first, one-at-a-time reintroduction, red flags and a written log, and both narrow claims under objection. B spends its turns on the mechanics of finding the cause: the cost of each retest, expectation bias in reading a patch test, and barrier-stacking as a cause no single test can catch. A spends two turns guessing at the user's motive (money) and then retracting the guess. B's ending also gives the user more conditions they can actually check.

comparisons.a_observation: The Subtractor invents a motive (the user paid for the products and wants to save the routine), and the Skeptic spends the next turn rejecting it because nothing in the user's words mentions money. Earlier, A.debate[3].text does narrow the plan well (test pairs because joint causes hide from single tests).
comparisons.b_observation: The Subtractor points to the real cost of each reintroduction. The Experimenter concedes that testing everything is greedy, but names the opposite risk (dropping a harmless product and keeping the guilty one) and narrows to prioritized small-patch trials. The Skeptic then attacks the trial itself through expectation bias and proposes writing down in advance what counts as a reaction.
comparisons.why_it_matters: The user asked how to find the cause. B's exchanges each improve the method the user will run. A's motive detour mostly cancels itself out.

comparisons.a_observation: Gives clear red flags, a calm-first step, a logged one-at-a-time reintroduction with pairs tested last, the option of simply dropping nonessential products, and dermatologist patch testing.
comparisons.b_observation: Gives red flags, prioritized reintroduction starting with the most valued product on a small area, and an observable check A lacks: if stinging continues a week or two after stopping all three, the cause is probably something else. It also suggests using fewer products at once if the reaction appears only when layering.
comparisons.why_it_matters: The 'persists after stopping' condition tells the user whether the product hypothesis survives at all, before any reintroduction starts.

comparisons.a_observation: Explicitly marks the mind's own extensions beyond the book ('my own addition to Taleb', 'go further than Taleb').
comparisons.b_observation: Lists the products, severity and other changes as unknowns. It also lists 'whether they were introduced together' as unknown, although the user's wording ('started three new skincare products last week') largely answers that.
comparisons.why_it_matters: A keeps the book's idea separate from the mind's extension more visibly. This is a smaller advantage that does not outweigh B's stronger interaction.

verdict.best_of_a: A.debate[3].text: The Controlled Tester takes the Skeptic's point that products may only irritate together and narrows his own method: test singly, then in pairs, and admit that joint causes are its weakest case.
verdict.best_of_b: B.debate[6].text: The Skeptic warns that expecting a product to be guilty can make a faint tingle feel like proof, and proposes writing down beforehand what counts as a reaction, along with the date, weather and other changes.

concerns.description: Speculates about a financial motive the user never stated. The next turn walks it back, but it still steers the self-reflection in A.clearer.
Treats whether the products were introduced together as unknown, although the user's wording implies they were started at roughly the same time.

verdict.reason: B's turns respond to each other more. Kahneman's claim narrows after Duke's objection, Thoreau's doubt about 'bet' gets a direct answer about reversibility, and the ending adds a correction for focusing on the new job. A drifts into guessing at the user's motives (security, escape, being valued) that the user never raised. B keeps the open questions tied to facts the user can check: how the commute is made, what the hours would displace, the after-tax gain, and how reversible the move is.

comparisons.a_observation: Thoreau dismisses the test week as 'a tourist's view'. Duke only narrows toward negotiation five turns later (A.debate[8].text), and in between A.debate[4].text grants a point for the raise without anything in the previous turn prompting it.
comparisons.b_observation: Duke points out that Kahneman's own misprediction point cuts both ways. Kahneman then narrows his claim to stop-and-go travel and keeps a caveat. Later Thoreau's objection to 'bet' (B.debate[6].text) is answered directly with reversibility as the deciding variable (B.debate[7].text).
comparisons.why_it_matters: The user gets claims that were tested and refined against each other, not positions that sit side by side.

comparisons.a_observation: A third mind suggests the 25% may be 'a verdict from other people on what you are worth' and that the user would be 'buying approval by the hour'. The user gave no hint of this; it is an invented motive turned into a branch.
comparisons.b_observation: Branches on what the hours would otherwise hold (sleep, a child at bedtime, exercise) and on whether the commute is a train or a drive. Both are things the user did not say and can check.
comparisons.why_it_matters: For a decision question, branching on observable facts helps the user more than speculating about hidden motives.

comparisons.a_observation: Gives sound conditions: a real financial gap, softening through negotiation, and checking whether a closer job would fix the same problem. It also suggests setting a limit in advance.
comparisons.b_observation: Gives conditions on commute mode, what the hours displace, financial relief or career path combined with reversibility, and the after-tax gain net of commuting costs. Each comes with a concrete way to learn it.
comparisons.why_it_matters: Both give the user a usable set of conditions. B is a little more concrete, but this does not decide the comparison.

verdict.best_of_a: A.debate[8].text: Recasting the test as negotiation (ask for remote days, a later start or a relocation allowance) is a cheap, high-information step. A.debate[10].text adds that staying is also a prediction.
verdict.best_of_b: B.debate[8].text: The warning that the new job is imagined vividly and the old one barely at all, plus the instruction to list the current job's downsides just as concretely, corrects a real bias in this comparison.

concerns.description: States a speculative psychological reading (seeking approval through the pay figure) about the user's motives with some certainty ('no commute is a good price'). It is conditional, but the input does not support it.

The point that the commute effect is strongest for unpredictable, stop-and-go travel, and the claim in B.debate[1].text that people adapt to pay but not to commutes, come from commuting research outside Thinking, Fast and Slow. Neither is marked as the mind's own extension.
'Adaptation cuts both ways' is followed by a sentence about commute adaptation that fits poorly with the argument for the raise, which makes the turn's logic hard to follow.

verdict.reason: Both debates interact well: claims narrow under objection and each ends with a stated disagreement. B keeps its turns on how the user can learn what this commute will actually be like. It brings in evidence from people who already make the trip, staying put as a real option, and a checkpoint that changes because of an objection. A spends much of its middle and its ending on motives read from the single word 'worth', which the user did not supply. A's hourly-rate test is excellent, but on balance B leaves the user with more observable conditions to check.

comparisons.a_observation: Turns 5 to 7 and 11 build the crux around two hypothesized motives, proof of worth or escape from a stuck job, inferred from the user's phrase 'worth it'. They are labeled as possibilities, but the closing turn makes them 'the important one'.
comparisons.b_observation: Turns 5 and 6 take apart facts the user did not give (train or traffic, 25% of what after tax and travel, remote days) and add the current job as the real comparison point, so 'staying put is a legitimate answer'.
comparisons.why_it_matters: The user asked how to decide. B's open questions are ones the user can check and that change the trade. A's central split rests on a psychological reading the input does not support.

comparisons.a_observation: The Accountant engages both rival readings and concedes a 'bounded' trial. The Auditor then attacks 'bounded' (turn 8), and the Bet Placer answers by making the exit concrete with a pre-set rule (turn 9). This is a tight chain of objection and answer.
comparisons.b_observation: The Auditor amends the checkpoint from early to six months with daily mood notes, for a stated reason (novelty hides costs), and the Exit Planner explicitly accepts the amendment (turn 11). In turn 8 the Skeptic turns the Auditor's adaptation argument back on him.
comparisons.why_it_matters: Both endings know more than their openings, and both disagreements are earned, so interaction does not separate them.

comparisons.a_observation: Two branches depend on the user's motive (valued or escaping). One observable step: ride the route and ask about remote days.
comparisons.b_observation: The branches turn on observable conditions: train or traffic, a defined use for the after-tax gain, time lost with people, and employer flexibility. The learning steps are proportionate: ride twice, talk to current commuters, write stopping criteria, keep a daily mood note.
comparisons.why_it_matters: B's conditions are ones the user can find out before deciding, which is what a decision question needs.

verdict.best_of_a: A.debate[3].text: The test of dividing the after-tax raise by about seven hundred commute hours, then asking whether you would accept that hourly wage for sitting in transit, turns the trade into one concrete number the user can judge.
verdict.best_of_b: B.debate[1].text: The Forecast Skeptic's point that people already doing a similar commute are better evidence than the user's imagination gives the user a cheap, specific way to reduce the core uncertainty.

concerns.description: The debate attributes a motive (needing proof of being valued, or fear of staying stuck) based on one word in the user's question. It is hedged as a possibility, but it ends up framing the ending and the dependsOn map.
The minds refer to each other by their source authors ('push back on Duke', 'Duke thinks'), which blurs the line between the fictional mind and the book.
The conditional map is one run-on paragraph, not separate condition-to-consequence lines, which makes it harder to scan.

The suggestion that people adapt to predictable commutes is hedged, but the commuting research usually cited suggests adaptation to commutes is weak. The mind presents it as a possibility, not a finding.

verdict.reason: Both debates follow nearly the same arc: an argument for speaking, an argument for letting it be, separating the fact from the story, a pause experiment rebutted as a hidden test, and a narrowed ending that offers a light, specific remark. A's distinct contribution is two competing readings of the user's sting that call for different actions. B's is the information-asymmetry exchange about whether the friend even knows the effort is lopsided, and it avoids inventing the friend's gender. Each is somewhat stronger on a different point, and neither advantage would change what the user takes away.

comparisons.a_observation: The Over-functioner Spotter notes that the 'worry about mattering' reading (turn 6) and the 'borrowed standard' reading (turn 7) point to different actions, and concedes speaking is not mandatory. The claim narrows because of the objection.
comparisons.b_observation: The Realist answers the Voice Advocate's 'gift of information' (turn 7) with the strongest objection available: the friend may know perfectly well and be content to be invited, so the information lands as pressure. This is then refined in turns 9 and 10 into an explicit disagreement over timing.
comparisons.why_it_matters: Both debates end knowing more than they began, by different routes. A looks inward at what the user wants. B looks at what the friend knows. Both are things this user needs to weigh.

comparisons.a_observation: Assigns the friend a gender ('she may be a low-initiation person'), which the user never gave, and keeps it throughout. It does use the user's own phrase 'nothing happens' (A.debate[5].text) to drive a reading.
comparisons.b_observation: Keeps the friend ungendered ('they') and names the unknown reasons (busy, shy, assuming you like organizing, less invested) as branches. It uses 'You said the meetings are lovely' (B.debate[1].text) to shape the argument.
comparisons.why_it_matters: An invented detail is small but shows less care with what the user actually said. It does not change any recommendation.

comparisons.a_observation: Ties the choice to which reading fits (mattering vs. contentment) and offers a sharp self-test in A.clearer: would the sting vanish if she initiated tomorrow?
comparisons.b_observation: Ties the choice to whether the effort feels like a burden. It offers both a pause and a scripted casual remark, and says the friend's response over time is the information.
comparisons.why_it_matters: Both give observable conditions and a low-stakes next step. A's self-test is a little sharper, and B's two options are a little broader.

verdict.best_of_a: A.debate[7].text: It makes the decision turn on which internal reading fits, and shows that each reading leads to a different action. That is the most clarifying move in either debate.
verdict.best_of_b: B.debate[7].text: The rebuttal that the friend may already know and be content to be invited directly tests the 'speaking is a gift of information' claim from the turn before. It is the debate's best piece of interaction.

concerns.description: The friend is referred to as 'she' throughout, but the user never gave the friend's gender.
The Fact-Story Separator speaks in two consecutive turns (turns 5 and 6), which breaks the turn-taking and makes one voice dominate the middle of the debate.

'Voice is cheaper than leaving' is attributed through Hirschman's framework, but Hirschman generally treats voice as costlier than exit. The extension of an organizational theory to a friendship is not flagged as the mind's own.

verdict.reason: Both debates find the same core split: is the user worn out by the effort, or unsure whether the friend cares? B gets there by reading the user's own words, and its positions narrow visibly under objection, ending in a concrete, observable middle option (a clear handover) that sits between saying nothing and having a talk. A is calibrated and well-behaved, but its exchanges converge more generically, and its key distinction arrives only at the end without anything to act on.

comparisons.a_observation: The Coach objects that a silent test is a trap. The Statistician concedes in A.debate[6].text and moves to wording, and the debate then mostly agrees to 'speak lightly'. The Philosopher's turn in A.debate[5].text largely adds a citation rather than moving the argument.
comparisons.b_observation: The Requester explicitly narrows from 'say something' (B.debate[0].text) to 'handover first, speech second', and gives the cause: the Realist's point in B.debate[8].text that a clear handover is easy to read while stopping is ambiguous. The Generous Friend's request-vs-demand objection in B.debate[7].text is answered rather than restated.
comparisons.why_it_matters: The user's own fallback, stopping texting, is exactly the ambiguous test. B replaces it with a readable one and shows why, so the ending knows more than the opening.

comparisons.a_observation: The effort-vs-being-wanted distinction is raised in the ninth turn and confirmed in the tenth, but A.dependsOn mostly maps it onto 'raise it kindly' versus 'ask a warm question', with similar actions on each branch.
comparisons.b_observation: The Realist ties the reading to the user's phrase 'always the one making plans' as a workload complaint. B.debate[6].text then gives a different sentence for each branch, and B.dependsOn adds a handover trial with a time frame as the step for when the answer is unknown.
comparisons.why_it_matters: The user asked whether to say something. B shows that what to say depends on which worry it is, and offers a low-cost step that produces observable evidence first.

comparisons.a_observation: The three voices are distinct, but several turns open by agreeing with the previous speaker ('I partly agree', 'The Coach has a point', 'Fine', 'Good'), which gives a somewhat uniform, consensual register.
comparisons.b_observation: The Generous Friend challenges both other speakers ('You're both keeping accounts') and holds a dissent to the end in B.debate[10].text, so the stakes differ across the three.
comparisons.why_it_matters: A dissent that survives to the end tells the user that accepting a lopsided friendship is a real option, not a rhetorical one.

verdict.best_of_a: A.debate[4].text: It clearly names why quietly going silent is a poor test: you will read the silence in whatever way hurts most. That directly protects the user from the move they hinted at.
verdict.best_of_b: B.debate[6].text: Two short, non-accusing scripts, one for doubt and one for workload, each tied to a different reading of the user's situation.

concerns.description: Throughout, B refers to the friend as 'she', but the user never gave the friend's gender. It is an invented detail, though it does not change the argument.

It offers a psychological reading of the user's motive (seeking proof they matter). It is explicitly framed as one the user can reject, and B.debate[5].text counters it with an equally plausible reading, so the certainty risk is low.

verdict.reason: Both debates separate feeling behind from wanting the milestones, test competing readings of the feeling (belonging versus expiring options or borrowed desire), narrow their claims under objection, and end with observable conditions. A is somewhat stronger on trust: it flags the limits of its own source and marks where a mind goes beyond its book. B is somewhat stronger on interaction and usefulness: the witness-bias objection widens the sample, and it splits the milestone label from the goods behind it. Neither edge would change what this user takes away.

comparisons.a_observation: The Experimenter admits that Ibarra studied career changers, not marriage, and so limits small trials to reversible choices. That produces the reversibility dividing line in A.debate[9].text.
comparisons.b_observation: The Detective objects that people who took the path are biased witnesses (sunk cost, imitation). The Forecaster answers in B.debate[4].text by widening the sample and separating the label from the goods it promises, and the Detective narrows his own claim in B.debate[9].text.
comparisons.why_it_matters: Each debate has a claim that clearly narrows under pressure and ends knowing more than it began. A's narrowing gives the user a rule for which choices to trial and which to wait on. B's gives a test of whether the milestone itself or what it stands for is the draw.

comparisons.a_observation: The phrase 'I would go further than Thoreau here' marks the belonging reading as the mind's own extension, and the critique of Ibarra's scope is calibrated.
comparisons.b_observation: The summary says the Detective treats present doubt as possibly the most honest signal, but the Detective mostly argued the feeling says little. In B.debate[7].text the Experimenter rejects withdrawing from friends, which the Detective never proposed.
comparisons.why_it_matters: These are small slips in B, but A keeps book and extension apart more cleanly. That helps a user deciding how much weight each voice deserves.

comparisons.a_observation: Its branches (drifting from friends, a real deadline, fading without comparison) end in a proportionate step: reversible experiments now, irreversible choices held until the wanting is the user's own.
comparisons.b_observation: Its branches include picturing the actual life versus the status, loss of shared time, a pull that fades when alone, and real time limits checked by talking to people on different paths, including those who chose none.
comparisons.why_it_matters: Both give conditions the user could observe. A's reversibility rule and B's label-versus-goods test are equally actionable, and both are grounded in the user's uncertainty about wanting these things.

verdict.best_of_a: A.debate[8].text: The Experimenter limits her own source's reach and draws the reversible-versus-irreversible line, which becomes the debate's most practical rule.
verdict.best_of_b: B.debate[4].text: Separating the milestone from the good it promises (a home as security, a wedding as being chosen) gives the user a concrete way to tell borrowed wanting from real wanting.

concerns.description: The summary describes the Detective as treating the user's present doubt as possibly the most honest signal, but the Detective's turns argue that the feeling says little and point to noticing private envy. The summary slightly misstates his position.
It brings in having a child, which the user never mentioned. It is framed as an example of an irreversible choice, not an assumed fact, so it does little harm.

verdict.reason: Both debates interact well and end knowing more than they began, but B introduces a rival reading of the 'behind' feeling (closeness with friends slipping) that changes another mind's advice and yields two readings with opposite observable predictions. That gives the user a more actionable conditional map. A's best move, that not-wanting can itself be borrowed, is sharp and directly relevant, but its ending converges on a looser blend of trials plus a suspicion check.

comparisons.a_observation: The Desire Detective argues that rejecting the milestones can be as borrowed as wanting them. The Realist concedes in A.debate[6] and pushes back on the 'suspicion spiral', which is a genuine exchange, though it ends in a fairly general synthesis.
comparisons.b_observation: The Experimenter's closeness reading makes the Desire Detective say it 'changes my advice'. The two readings predict opposite things (relief when apart versus relief when together), and B.debate[8] turns the experiment toward company rather than property.
comparisons.why_it_matters: The user can tell the two readings apart by watching their own reactions, and each points to a different action. A's narrowing is real but leaves the user with less to tell apart.

comparisons.a_observation: Takes the user's 'not sure I even want' seriously by questioning the doubt itself, not only the want.
comparisons.b_observation: Uses 'most of my friends' to suggest that the loss is shared ground and free evenings, not the houses. B.debate[10] and B.debate[11] also take seriously that 'not sure' can be a legitimate end state after trying.
comparisons.why_it_matters: Each debate draws a different, real implication from the user's own words, so neither clearly wins here.

comparisons.a_observation: Its branches turn on whether the pull survives privacy and whether the 'no' appears mainly around friends. Useful, but the actions are mostly 'trials' or 'stay the course'.
comparisons.b_observation: Its branches map to distinct actions: less exposure, investing in friendships, time-limited trials of a specific want, or accepting 'not sure'. Each has an observable trigger.
comparisons.why_it_matters: For a decision question, distinct actions tied to observable conditions are more usable than a general recommendation to experiment.

verdict.best_of_a: A.debate[5].text: The point that declaring you don't want the milestones can be reactive, 'keeps the crowd at the center', directly tests the user's uncertainty instead of taking it at face value.
verdict.best_of_b: B.debate[6].text: The Desire Detective accepts the closeness reading, revises its advice, and states the opposite predictions that would tell the two readings apart.

concerns.description: The situation summary and B.debate[4].text refer to 'the user' in the third person rather than addressing the reader, which reads less naturally.
'Ibarra notes that who we spend time with shapes who we become' loosely paraphrases Working Identity's theme of shifting connections. It is plausible, but the wording is not verified.

verdict.reason: Both debates reach the same multi-cause picture (westerlies, ocean heat storage, currents, Rockies-steered flow), but A gets there through a tighter chain of objections, ending with the Newfoundland-versus-Norway challenge that heat storage alone cannot answer. A also closes with three competing explanations, each paired with the evidence that would separate it from the others. B spends its middle third (turns 6-9) speculating about whether the asker is afraid of Europe freezing. That turns an explanatory question into a question about the user's motive and leaves less room for the mechanism.

comparisons.a_observation: Turns 6-10 stay on the mechanism. Heat storage is challenged on the grounds that it 'does not explain why Europe beats Newfoundland', which leads to the contrast in arriving water and then to the mountains suspect.
comparisons.b_observation: Turns 6-9 move to why the user is asking ('Maybe what's behind your question is a fear you've seen in headlines'), and the conditional map is organized by user motive rather than by competing explanations.
comparisons.why_it_matters: The user asked why the temperature contrast exists. A uses its turns to sharpen the competing causes. B spends about a third of its turns on a guess about the user's psychology that the question does not invite.

comparisons.a_observation: The Conveyor Theorist raises the strongest objection to the storage-plus-winds account: two ocean-facing coasts differ, so storage cannot explain the gap. The Physicist answers it directly ('Partly yes... matters locally') before adding the Rockies. Both ocean minds then narrow their claims explicitly (turns 9-10), and the Conveyor Theorist reframes his claim as about stability rather than present-day mildness.
comparisons.b_observation: The early exchange is good. The 'delivery truck and warehouse' rebuttal and the Vancouver plus Rockies test in turn 4 make the Mapper narrow his claim in turn 5. After that, the narrowing in turns 9-10 is driven by the fear framing rather than by new physical evidence.
comparisons.why_it_matters: A's ending knows more than its opening about the physics. B's ending mostly knows that the question has two possible motives.

comparisons.aspect: Usefulness: what would separate the explanations
comparisons.a_observation: It gives three hypotheses, each with an observable prediction: mildness tracking ocean heat transport, any coast downwind of open ocean being mild, and model runs with the Rockies flattened. It adds coastal-versus-inland comparisons on both oceans.
comparisons.b_observation: Its branches are keyed to what the user wants to know, and its only test is to look for recent reviews comparing ocean and atmospheric heat transport.
comparisons.why_it_matters: For exploration, the user needs distinctions that discriminate between causes. A's map gives these directly.

verdict.best_of_a: A.debate[7].text: The Newfoundland-versus-Norway objection exposes exactly what heat storage cannot explain, and the remaining turns have to answer it.
verdict.best_of_b: B.debate[3].text: The Air Skeptic combines the Vancouver counterexample and the Rockies-steered cold outbreaks into one compact test that makes the Gulf-Stream-only story give ground.

concerns.description: A mind speculates that the user's question hides a fear seen in headlines. This is offered tentatively, and Turn 8 hands the choice back to the user, but it projects a psychological motive onto a plain physics question.

'A current is sufficient to explain some of Europe, but maybe not necessary' is loosely phrased: the Pacific counterexample bears on necessity for mildness in general, not on Europe specifically. The point survives, but the logic is imprecise.

Both debates attribute much of the contrast to mountain-steered stationary waves (A explicitly labels this as the mind's own extension; B's Air Skeptic says he would 'push further than the textbook'). That attribution reflects real but debated research, and neither debate can verify it from the input.

verdict.reason: Both debates move from the single-cause Gulf Stream story to a combination of causes, and both narrow claims under objection. B stays on the physical mechanism the whole way and adds a real distinguishing factor: air reaching eastern Canada has crossed a cold continent, and mountains bend the wind pattern. A gives roughly four of its eleven turns to guessing what the user wants psychologically, which is the forced personal framing an exploratory question should avoid.

comparisons.a_observation: From Turn 7 to Turn 10, A stops arguing about mechanism and starts reading the user: 'perhaps they want one clean cause to hold onto', then an 'apparent unfairness' reading, and the Energy Accountant says these readings change what he would say. The ending conditions in A.dependsOn are framed around what the user wants, not around physical evidence.
comparisons.b_observation: B's middle turns stay on the mechanism. 'Same wind, different history' contrasts westerlies that cross ocean with westerlies that cross a continent, and B.debate[5].text adds seasonal heat storage and the Rockies steering cold air over eastern North America.
comparisons.why_it_matters: The user asked an explanatory question. B spends its turns on factors that actually separate the explanations, while A spends a third of its debate on guesses about the user's motives that the question does not invite.

comparisons.a_observation: A's early exchanges are tight. Wind is the delivery truck and the current is the cargo (Turns 2 to 3), and Turn 6 correctly points out that abrupt past change cannot establish how large the current's share is today, which makes the Fragility Watcher narrow his claim in Turn 7.
comparisons.b_observation: B also narrows claims under objection. Turn 4 separates 'past collapses show the ocean can matter' from 'it is the main cause today'. Turn 7 trades concessions explicitly and gives the cause. Turn 9 separates measuring a warm current from showing that it causes the mild winters. B's concessions build toward a fuller causal picture instead of drifting off topic.
comparisons.why_it_matters: Both debates answer objections, but B ends knowing more about the physics (continental air, mountains, storage), while A ends knowing more about possible user motives.

comparisons.a_observation: A names a good discriminating test: model comparisons that change ocean heat transport or the winds while holding everything else fixed. Its other branches are framed as what the user wants.
comparisons.b_observation: B gives a concise mechanistic answer the user can state, ties the size of the ocean's share to future risk, and names the same kind of with-and-without-ocean-heat-transport model test.
comparisons.why_it_matters: Both name the test that would settle the open question, so this does not decide between them.

verdict.best_of_a: A.debate[5].text: The Energy Accountant's objection that abrupt-change evidence cannot settle how large the current's share is today is the sharpest single move in either debate, and it makes the opponent narrow his claim.
verdict.best_of_b: B.debate[4].text: 'Same wind, different history' is the clearest statement of the central asymmetry: Europe's westerlies cross ocean while eastern Canada's cross a cold continent. Turn 6 builds on it with storage and mountain effects.

concerns.description: Speculative readings of the user's motives ('wants one clean cause', 'bothered by an apparent unfairness') are imposed on a purely explanatory question. They are offered as possibilities, but they take attention away from the mechanism.
A leaves out the role of mountain ranges and atmospheric wave patterns in delivering continental cold air to eastern Canada, a factor commonly cited in this debate.
Both summaries add a self-reflection about why a single cause feels satisfying. It is mild and offered tentatively, but an exploratory physical question does not need it.
